21352-fragments-of-two-centuries-glimpse:
Alfred Kingston published these fragments in Royston in 1893, glimpses of country life when George the Third was king. His materials come chiefly from the Royston district in Hertfordshire, Cambridgeshire, and Essex, drawn from old parish papers and local records. An appendix tracks the rise and fall of rural population in forty-five parishes from 1801 to 1891.

Kingston admits the local colour but claims the picture stands for rural England generally. Court days under James I at Royston, fairs, work, and parish life fill his fragments. The book is a local historian's rescue of everyday detail: what people ate, earned, feared, and celebrated before the villages emptied.
27801-children-of-borneo:
Edwin H. Gomes, author of Seventeen Years Among the Sea Dyaks of Borneo, wrote this children's book on the Dyak peoples of Borneo, published in Edinburgh and London with eight colored illustrations. It draws on his earlier book with permission from its publishers.

Chapters cover village houses, babies and children, head-hunting, feasts, witch doctors, omens, marriages, and burials, with a Dyak legend retold. Written for young readers, the book introduces Borneo's jungles and peoples with the earnest, missionary-era tone of its series. Illustrations include a Dyak village house, girls weaving, a girl in gala costume, and a youth killing birds with a blow-pipe.
2863-satires-of-circumstance-lyrics-and-:
Thomas Hardy's Satires of Circumstance gathers lyrics and reveries first published in 1914, in the Macmillan edition of 1919 used here. The contents include Channel Firing, The Convergence of the Twain, The Ghost of the Past, and When I Set Out for Lyonnesse. Hardy's poems here are short, musical, and often spoken by ghosts, soldiers, or lovers looking back.

Irony rules the collection, since small choices and accidents undo large hopes. A speaker regrets masteries he might have gained and finds comfort only in having refrained, while a tomb waits at the end of the thought. The book shows Hardy's late lyric voice at its most controlled, pairing country scenes with a bleak sense of fate.
30233-folk-lore-in-borneo:
William Henry Furness offers a short sketch of folk lore among the peoples of Borneo, privately printed at Wallingford, Pennsylvania, in 1899. A Kayan chief fronts the monograph, and Furness warns at once that he gives a sketch only, not a full survey. Borneo is large, its peoples are scattered and cut off by constant inter-tribal warfare, and they differ in language, customs, and appearance more than Germans, French, or English differ.

No written language exists, Furness notes, not even picture drawings on rocks to guide a search for ancient myths. He calls the islanders savages of a high order, in the period language of his day, with a civilization above what the term usually implies. Modern readers should take the sketch as a dated field note, valuable for what one observer recorded, not as a final word on Borneo.
7222-fra-bartolommeo:
Leader Scott's Fra Bartolommeo, re-edited by Horace Shipp and Flora Kendrick, looks past the three great names of the Renaissance, Michelangelo, Leonardo, and Raphael, toward the fine artists who worked beside them. Fra Bartolommeo links with Andrea d'Agnolo in this study, and Scott argues that a host of exquisite painters deserve a place beside the giants.

The foreword sets that case plainly: fame has crowded out worthy neighbours, and this book restores one of them to view. Reproductions from official photographs of national collections help the reader judge the work. Scott writes with a connoisseur's care, tracing a painter's life through pictures rather than legend.
britannica-1911-bagnacavallo-bartolommeo:
Bagnacavallo, Bartolommeo (1484-1542), was an Italian painter whose real name was Ramenghi; his byname came from the little village of his birth. He studied first under Francia, then went to Rome and became a pupil of Raphael, working with many others on the Vatican gallery's decoration.

Back in Bologna, Bagnacavallo quickly took the leading place among its artists, and the entry credits him with great improvements in the whole Bolognese school's style. His design was held weaker than some Raphael-school work, but rich colouring and graceful drawing set him apart. Guido Reni and the Carracci studied and partly copied him. His best pieces named are a Dispute of St Augustine and a Madonna and Child, both at Bologna.
britannica-1911-bandello-matteo:
Matteo Bandello (1480–1562) was an Italian novelist, born at Castelnuovo, near Tortona, about 1480. Carefully educated, he entered the church without much zeal for theology. For many years he lived at Mantua and supervised the education of the famed Lucrezia Gonzaga, in whose honour he wrote a long poem.

The battle of Pavia cost Bandello his Milan house, burned, and his property, seized, when Lombardy fell to the emperor. He fled with Cesare Fregoso, an Italian general in French service, into France, and in 1550 he became bishop of Agen. His fame rests on his Novelle, tales printed in 1554 and 1573. The 1911 Britannica entry places them beside Boccaccio's Decameron, tracing the whole kind back to old French fabliaux.
britannica-1911-bandinelli-bartolommeo:
Bartolommeo Bandinelli, also called Baccio (1493–1560), was a Florentine sculptor, son of an eminent goldsmith who taught him the first elements of drawing. A strong bent for the fine arts took him early to Rustici, a sculptor and friend of Leonardo da Vinci, under whom he advanced fast.

Jealousy ruled his life, the entry says: of Benvenuto Cellini, and of Michelangelo, one of whose cartoons he is said to have torn up and destroyed. Some rank him second in sculpture only to Michelangelo. The 1911 Britannica entry points to his Hercules and Cacus in Florence and his reliefs in the cathedral choir there. It also names his copy of the Laocoon, and the figures of Christ and Nicodemus on his own tomb.
britannica-1911-borghesi-bartolommeo:
Bartolommeo Borghesi (1781–1860) was an Italian scholar of coins and inscriptions who laid firm ground under Roman dating. Born at Savignano near Rimini, he studied at Bologna and Rome. Study of medieval documents hurt his eyes, so he turned to epigraphy and numismatics. At Rome he sorted and catalogued coin collections, among them the Vatican's, for Pius VII.

The troubles of 1821 drove him to retire to San Marino, where he served for a time as podestà and died in 1860. His great work, Nuovi Frammenti dei Fasti Consolari Capitolini (1818–1820), gave scholars solid bases for the order of Roman history. Before his death he planned a full collection of all Latin inscriptions. Berlin's academy took the plan up under Mommsen, and the result was the Corpus Inscriptionum Latinarum.
britannica-1911-carducci-bartolommeo:
Bartolommeo Carducci (1560–1610) was an Italian painter. In Spain he was better known as Carducho. This 1911 Britannica entry gives his career. He was born in Florence and studied there. Ammanati taught him architecture and sculpture. Zuccaro taught him painting in the same city. He followed Zuccaro to Madrid in his service. There he painted the ceiling of the Escorial library.

Carducci also helped with the Escorial cloister frescoes. He was a great favourite with Philip III of Spain. He lived and died in Spain, where his works remain. His most celebrated picture is a Descent from the Cross. It hangs in San Felipe el Real, in Madrid. The entry closes with his younger brother Vincenzo. Vincenzo followed him to Madrid and painted for two kings. His best pictures decorated the Prado for Philip III. For years he taught painting in Madrid. His pupils carried the Spanish school forward in the 1600s.
britannica-1911-cicisbeo:
Cicisbeo is an Italian term, of uncertain origin, used from the 17th century onwards for a dangler about women. It may be an inversion of bel cece, beautiful chick-pea, or come from the French chiche beau with the same meaning. The cicisbeo was the professed gallant of a married woman in the custom described. He attended her at all public entertainments as her regular escort through the social round.

Fashion made the husband's absence part of the arrangement, since it was considered unfashionable for the husband to be escort. The cicisbeo's role was thus open and professed, not a hidden affair in the entry's account. He dangled about the lady in public, at entertainments where company expected to see him at her side. Word origin, two guesses at it, and that one social duty make up the facts this notice offers.
britannica-1911-jud-leo: Leo Jud (1482–1542), known to his own age as Meister Leu, was a Swiss reformer born in Alsace and schooled at Basel. He first studied medicine, then turned to theology under the sway of Zwingli. After four years as pastor of Einsiedeln, from 1518 to 1522, he became Zwingli's colleague at Zürich. His chief work was as a translator: he was the leading spirit in the Zürich Bible and made a Latin version of the Old Testament. He died at Zürich on the 19th of June 1542.
britannica-1911-langreo:
Langreo is a town of northern Spain in the province of Oviedo, set in steep hill country on the left bank of the river Nalon. A branch rail line runs from Oviedo to Labiana through the town. The count for 1900 gave 18,714 people, a large total for a place of its kind.

Farms round the town yield wheat, hemp, fruit, and cider in good amounts. Coal and iron mines nearby feed foundries, and mills turn out coarse cloth. Mining and making, rather than farming alone, explain the town's size, and the short account rests on those twin supports: rich ground below the hills and busy works beside the river.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-andrea-borrom:
The son of Count Giulio Cesare Borromeo, Andrea Borromeo was an Italian missionary born at or near Milan in the first half of the seventeenth century; he died in 1683. He entered the Theatine order in 1637. In 1652 he went to Mingrelia and Georgia, in Russian Transcaucasia, as a missionary, and worked there with success for eleven years to convert the people.

Back in Rome, he was chosen procurator for these missions, the agent handling their business at the centre. He turned down a bishopric, choosing mission work over rank. He left an account of his order's missions in those lands, a relazione on Georgia, Mingrelia, and the Theatine mission there, printed at Rome in 1704.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-antonio-tebal:
Ferrara poet Antonio Tebaldeo, born in 1463 and dead in 1537, changed his family name Tebaldi to a Latin form. He tutored Isabella d'Este and served as secretary to Lucrezia Borgia. Then he became a regular at the court of Pope Leo X in Rome, enjoying that scholarly pope's favour and the company of learned men and artists. He lost all his money in the sack of Rome in 1527 and lived the rest of his life in narrow circumstances.

He wrote verse in Latin and Italian, yet his Italian verse is faulted here more for faults of diction and style than praised for poetic power. With artificial manner, abuse of metaphor, and studied imagery, he foreshadowed Marinism, the extravagant seventeenth-century style also called Secentismo. He is also credited with reshaping Poliziano's Orfeo toward classical rules, and he joined debates on the nature of literary Italian.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-borneo:
Borneo's Catholic missions split between a Dutch prefecture in the south and a British prefecture in the north. Dutch Borneo left the vast Batavia vicariate on 11 February 1905 as a separate Capuchin prefecture, covering 204,633 square miles. Jesuits had visited its Catholics twice a year, and Father de Vriez built a church at Singkawang in 1875, while an interior station at Sedjiram rose and fell for lack of priests.

By 1906 the Dutch prefecture counted 8 Capuchin priests, 4 brothers, and 396 Catholics: 210 Chinese, 100 Dyaks, and 86 Europeans. Its stations stood at Singkawang and Sedjiram, with new posts at Samarinda and Pamangkat. British North Borneo and Labuan trace their mission to Father Ventimiglia, a Theatine sent by Innocent XI in 1687, though that early mission left no trace on the island.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-brother-leo:
Brother Leo, confessor, secretary, and constant companion of Saint Francis, guarded the saint's ideal of poverty after his death. A native of Assisi, though some writers say Viterbo, he joined Francis soon after the first Rule's approval in 1209 and was perhaps already a priest. From about 1220 he never left Francis's side, joining him at Fonte Colombo in 1223 to rewrite the rule and at Rome to seek its approval.

On La Verna in 1224 he witnessed the stigmata and wrote his plain account across Francis's autograph blessing, still kept at Assisi. Francis called him Frate Pecorello di Dio, God's little sheep-brother, for his simplicity. Leo nursed the dying saint, sang the Canticle of the Sun with Angelo at his bedside, and later smashed Elias's money vase for the basilica, earning a whipping and exile from Assisi.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-congregation-:
Victor Cangiano's entry follows the Missionaries of Saint Charles Borromeo, founded by John Baptist Scalabrini, Bishop of Piacenza, dead 1 June 1905. Leo XIII approved it in principle in 1887, and Propaganda definitively approved its constitution in 1908. Italian emigrants waiting in Milan's railway station pressed their spiritual and temporal needs on Scalabrini. Encouraged by Cardinal Simeoni, he bought a Piacenza residence, turning it into the Christopher Columbus Apostolic Institution, nucleus of a new congregation.

Seven priests and three lay brothers left Italy on 12 July 1888. Two priests and one brother sailed for New York, five priests and two brothers for Brazil. In New York they soon secured a Centre Street site among Italian colonists. Growth followed. Fathers now hold thirteen parish churches, mostly with schools, and two orphanages. The United States provinces count forty-five priests and three lay brothers, Brazil's single province thirty-five priests and five brothers. Emigrant care stays its heart.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cuneo:
A diocesan entry sketches Cuneo, capital of its Piedmont province, set on a hill between the Stura and Gesso rivers and suffragan to Turin. Originally part of the Diocese of Mondovi, it became an episcopal see in 1817 under Pius VII. Its cathedral is very ancient and beautiful, remodelled in the sixteenth century.

Over the main altar hangs a painting of St. John the Baptist and St. Michael by the Jesuit Father Pozzi, who also painted the ceiling of St. Ignatius in Rome. The first bishop was Amadeo Bruno di Samone. The diocese counted 111,200 people, 61 parishes, 190 churches and chapels, 240 priests, and 13 educational institutions at the time of writing.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-federico-borr:
Federico Borromeo was cardinal and archbishop of Milan from 1595 to 1631. Cousin and successor of St Charles, he was born in 1564. Made cardinal at twenty-three, he led the great diocese of Milan for thirty-six years. He preached tirelessly and reformed abuses among clergy and laity.

In the famine and plague of 1627 he fed two thousand poor daily at his gates. Nearly a hundred of his clergy died serving the sick. Manzoni immortalised his devotion in The Betrothed's pages. He founded the Ambrosian Library, opened in 1609 as a public library for all.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-felino-maria-:
Felino Maria Sandeo was an Italian canonist of the fifteenth century. Born at Felina in 1444, he taught canon law at Ferrara and Pisa. In 1484 he became auditor of the Sacred Palace at Rome. He became bishop of Penna and Atri in 1495, then coadjutor and bishop of Lucca.

Felino was a good compiler, though he lacked originality as a writer. His chief work comments at length on books one, two, four, and five of the Decretals. It appeared at Milan, Basle, and Lyons across the sixteenth century. He died at Lucca in October 1503, by most accounts.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-fra-bartolomm:
Fra Bartolommeo, born Bartolommeo di Pagholo del Fattorillo near Florence in 1475 and dead there in 1517. He was a Dominican painter who carried Renaissance art from its early phase toward its high splendour. Trained in the studio of Cosimo Rosselli, he formed a business partnership with Mariotto Albertinelli. He admired the reformer Savonarola so deeply that, after Savonarola's death in 1498, he entered the Dominican order himself.

His early fresco of the Last Judgment at Santa Maria Nuova already shows new freedom of pose and perspective. Later masterpieces in Florence and Lucca include a Madonna with St. Stephen and John the Baptist and a Descent from the Cross. They are praised for finely graded suffering softened by heavenly peace. The entry treats him as a painter of dignity, strong drawing, and quiet spiritual feeling rather than showy display.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giovanni-anto:
Giovanni Antonio Amadeo, also spelled Omodeo, was an Italian architect and sculptor born near Pavia in 1447, who died at Milan in 1522. In 1466 he began work with his brother Protasio at the Certosa near Pavia. A follower of Bramantino, he stands for the Lombard Renaissance, cutting deep into marble and folding drapery in flat, papery pleats. A Catholic Encyclopedia article ranks him with the great Tuscans of his time.

At the Certosa he carved the beautiful door from church to cloister, still called the door of Amadeo, and many reliefs for tomb facades. He designed the Colleoni chapel tomb at Bergamo and, from 1490, the Certosa facade itself. As joint architect of the Certosa and the cathedrals of Pavia and Milan, he pressed a Gothic cupola for Milan against strong opposition, and the work stopped in 1503.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gloria-in-exc:
Gloria in excelsis Deo is the great doxology, or angel's hymn, in the Mass, a version of a very old Greek form. It opens with the words sung by the angels at Christ's birth in Luke 2:14, to which other verses were added very early to form a doxology. A Catholic Encyclopedia article traces a hymn that reaches back at least to the third century.

A similar form appears in the Codex Alexandrinus of the fifth century. Pseudo-Athanasius used it before the fourth century. Extended and corrected of subordinationist traces, it is sung by the Byzantine Church at the Orthros with more verses than the Latin, ending with the Trisagion. Tradition says Saint Hilary of Poitiers translated it into Latin, perhaps learning it during his eastern exile in 360, though others credit Telesphorus or Symmachus.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gonzalo-de-be:
Gonzalo de Berceo was a Spanish poet active between 1220 and 1242, apparently the earliest Castilian author known to us by name. Born in the closing years of the twelfth century, he became a priest. He spent his whole life in or near the monastery of San Millán de la Cogolla. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows a poet who wrote for the common man.

His compositions run to more than thirteen thousand Alexandrine verses in monorhymed quatrains, the cuaderna via. They are religious and hagiographical: lives of Santo Domingo de Silos, San Millán, and Santa Oria, poems to the Virgin, and didactic works on the Mass and the signs of judgment. Following Latin sources with little originality, he writes in the vernacular and adopts the popular minstrel's methods to reach the popular heart.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-michelozzo-di:
Michelozzo di Bartolommeo, architect and sculptor born at Florence about 1391, died in 1472. He wielded a quiet but far-reaching influence in the early Renaissance, and for over a decade worked with Donatello, to whom several of Michelozzo's works have been wrongly ascribed. The Aragazzi monument in Montepulciano Cathedral and the Brancacci tomb at Naples are Michelozzo's alone, while he helped Donatello execute John XXIII's tomb.

He also modelled several brass pieces for Donatello, with whom he worked on a pulpit for Prato Cathedral. Ghiberti drew important help from him on his Matthew and on Florence Cathedral's bronze sacristy door. Among other Florence works, a silver St. John, later copied larger in clay, is certainly his alone, while others are his with more or less probability. At San Giorgio Maggiore in Venice a wooden crucifix by him still survives. As architect he stands worthy of comparison with Brunelleschi.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-montevideo:
Montevideo, the archdiocese covering all of Uruguay, passed from Paraguayan church jurisdiction until 1620, then Buenos Aires, until Rome made it a vicariate apostolic in 1828. It rose to a bishopric in 1878 under Hyacinth Vera as first bishop. In 1897 it became an archdiocese, with suffragan sees at Melo and Salto planned but still unfilled in 1910.

The Church suffered persecution after colonial days, worst under Santos between 1880 and 1890. He barred religious under forty from vows, imposed civil marriage and criminalised baptism before civil registration. By the entry's time it flourished again, with 46 parishes, 122 priests, some 100 churches and chapels, and over 300 nuns teaching and serving the poor, under Archbishop Mariano Soler.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-paulinus-a-s-:
Paulinus a Sancto Bartholomaeo, born Philip Wesdin at Hoff in Lower Austria on 25 April 1748 and dead at Rome on 7 January 1806, was a missionary and Orientalist. Entering the Carmelites, he was sent in 1774 to Malabar in India, where he became his order's vicar general and apostolic visitor. Recalled to Rome in 1789 to report on the mission, he was charged with editing books for missionaries.

Political troubles kept him at Vienna from 1798 to 1800, and he returned to Rome as prefect of studies at Propaganda. His many learned books on the East were highly prized in their day and advanced knowledge of Indian letters and life. He gave the world its first printed Sanskrit grammar. Chief works include his 1791 Brahmanic system from Borgia museum monuments, his 1792 critical survey of Propaganda's Indian codices, and his 1796 Voyage to the East Indies.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sisters-of-me:
The Sisters of Mercy of Saint Borromeo began as a pious association of ladies formed in 1626 to care for the sick in the hospital of Saint Charles at Nancy. A generous endowment from the father of Emmanuel Chauvenel, a young advocate who gave his life serving the sick, helped constitute them a religious community in 1652. Their rule, based on that of Saint Augustine, won papal approbation in 1859.

Under persecution the sisters kept their work so bravely that they won praise even from their persecutors. On 22 July 1804 they resumed their religious habit, gained Napoleon's approval, and soon flourished again. Additional constitutions were confirmed by Leo XIII in 1892. Their work covers trade and domestic schools, homes for first communicants, protectories, poor-houses, homes for the disabled, reformatories, schools, and nursing the sick in their homes.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-society-of-st:
Founded at Bonn in 1845 by Franz Xavier Dieringer, August Reichensperger, and Max von Loe, the Society of Saint Charles Borromeo is a German Catholic association spreading edifying, instructive, and entertaining literature. Placed under the episcopate's protection, it spread across Germany, counting 145,250 members in 258 main societies and 3,247 branches by mid-1907. Its chief office stands at Bonn.

Each member receives books yearly as a gift, in quantity matching the society's means and dues from 75 or 38 cents to 1.50 dollars a year. Surplus funds found libraries, over 3,000 by 1904, and aid workingmen's, people's, asylum, and hospital libraries. Its 1906 catalogue held over 10,000 titles for purchase, and since 1902 it issues the periodical Die Bücherwelt. Free reading rooms serve the public in larger cities.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-bernard-to:
St. Bernard Tolomeo was founder of the congregation of the Blessed Virgin of Monte Oliveto, born at Siena, Tuscany, in 1272. He died in 1348. This entry follows a boy baptized Giovanni, who took the name Bernard out of admiration for the saintly abbot of Clairvaux. His uncle Christopher Tolorneo, a Dominican, educated him. He desired religious life, but his father's opposition prevented it, and he continued his studies in secular surroundings.

After philosophy and mathematics he turned to civil and canon law, and to theology. Bernard then served for a time in Rudolph of Hapsburg's armies. Back in Siena, his fellow citizens appointed him to the highest town offices. While thus occupied he was struck with blindness. Having recovered his sight through the Blessed Virgin's intervention, he retired in 1313 to a solitary spot ten miles from Siena, where he led a life of prayer.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-charles-bo:
St. Charles Borromeo was archbishop of Milan, cardinal-priest of St. Prassede, papal secretary of state under Pius IV, and a chief factor in the Catholic Counter-Reformation. This entry follows a boy born in Arona castle, a town on Lake Maggiore's southern shore in northern Italy, on 2 October 1538. He died at Milan on 3 November 1584. His emblem is the crowned word humilitas, part of the Borromeo shield.

He is usually shown in art in cardinal's robes, barefoot, carrying the archbishop's cross, with a rope round his neck and one hand raised in blessing. That recalls his work during the plague. His feast falls on 4 November. His father, Count Giberto Borromeo, married Margherita de Medici about 1530. Her younger brother, Giovanni Angelo, Cardinal de' Medici, became pope in 1559 as Pius IV. Charles was the second son, and third of six children, of Giberto and Margherita.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-viatora-cocca:
Viatora Coccaleo, named for his birthplace Coccaglio in Lombardy, was a Capuchin friar and theologian who died in 1793. For a time he lectured in theology, and his books won him a place among the noteworthy theologians of an age of theological decline.

His works include Tentamina theologico-scholastica from Bergamo, a synopsis of moral theology from Venice, and Instituta moralia from Milan. Best known is his defence of papal supremacy, Italus ad Justinum Febronium, a leading reply to Febronius. He also wrote against Jansenism, joined the debates on devotion to the Sacred Heart and on sanctifying holy days raised by the Synod of Pistoia in 1786. Studied the text and meaning of Prosper of Aquitaine's poem Against the Ungrateful.
doe-osti-2572890-poisson-equation-for-a-:
A Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory paper by Chad Mitchell, dated July 23, 2025, solves a classic problem for accelerator physics. Inside a uniformly filled ellipsoid, the Poisson equation governs the space charge fields that push a particle beam apart. Earlier treatments handled upright ellipsoids, aligned with the axes. Mitchell treats the general case, a tilted ellipsoid with arbitrary correlations, in any number of dimensions.

The central result is an explicit formula tying the matrix of the quadratic space charge potential straight to the ellipsoid's covariance matrix. For two and three dimensions, that formula yields the linear map for a space charge kick. The kick advances the beam's six-by-six covariance matrix during envelope tracking, the fast simulation mode used to follow beam size along a machine. An appendix gives the general free-space solution in dimension d for sources with ellipsoidal symmetry.
doe-osti-2573097-improved-chopper-system:
Oak Ridge report ORNL/TM-2025/3951, by Georg Ehlers in July 2025, designs an improved chopper system for a neutron spectrometer at the planned Second Target Station. The instrument is CHESS, a compact spectrometer for small samples proposed in 2021. Choppers are spinning gates that slice the neutron beam into pulses of chosen energy. At a low-repetition-rate source, the pulse pattern decides what the instrument can measure.

The proposed cascade does three things older setups cannot combine. It selects a variable number of pulses per frame, spaces the chosen pulses with growing timing gaps, and widens each pulse in turn. Together those tricks hold energy resolution roughly even across wavelengths within one frame. Sections detail the M-chopper and H-chopper hardware and present simulation results for the cascade. The report updates the instrument's 2023 technical design with a concrete chopper plan.
fra-bartolommeo:
Leader Scott's Fra Bartolommeo, with Andrea d'Agnolo, treats two painters of the High Renaissance who worked beside its giants. The foreword notes how Michelangelo, Leonardo and Raphael draw our minds away from the many fine painters beside them, yet exquisite painters stand among that host.

Fra Bartolommeo links the religious art of the preceding period, through Masaccio and Piero di Cosimo, to the modern painters of the Renaissance itself. Scott, re-edited by Horace Shipp and Flora Kendrick, follows his work with reproductions from official photographs. Readers of Renaissance art will find this a useful, sympathetic study of a transition painter.
podcast-tuckercarlson-omBSEuFTYEo:
Congressman Thomas Massie of Kentucky talks deep state secrets and off-grid living with Tucker Carlson. Massie is known as one of the most independent voices in Congress, often voting alone on principle. At home he built a house that runs without public power or water.

Massie shares what he has learned about how Washington really works behind the scenes. He then teaches the basics of his off-grid life, from solar power to growing food. Carlson, an admirer, draws out both the politics and the practical skills. Free-minded viewers get liberty preached and practiced by the same man.
podcast-tuckercarlson-t2O-kg2vCEo:
Media host Glenn Beck joins Tucker Carlson to talk about Bible prophecy, the fight against evil, and why he says alcoholics will save the world. Beck is a radio and TV host who has spoken in the open about his past drinking.

Beck tells how he hit the floor as a drunk and how faith pulled him up. He argues that men who beat drink learn the grit the country now needs. Carlson draws out his read of prophecy and the age. Listeners get Beck raw and fervent. The library keeps the talk as a record, and it notes the title's wider claim on drinkers.
podcast-tuckercarlson-zdbqUoTyReo:
Tucker Carlson turns to humor with a look at the Babylon Bee's odd record. The satire site writes joke headlines that later come true. That streak gives the episode its hook.

Carlson lists cases where real news matched old Bee jokes. He argues the jokes land because they start from true trends. The site, in his telling, reads the culture better than straight news. The hour stays light, with clips and laughs. It still makes a point: when satire predicts the news, the news itself may be the strangest joke of all.
satires-of-circumstance-lyrics-and-rever: Thomas Hardy wrote Satires of Circumstance, Lyrics and Reveries, with Miscellaneous Pieces, transcribed from the 1919 Macmillan edition in London. Copyright lines give a first edition of 1914, reprinted in 1915 and 1919, with a pocket edition in 1919. The contents open with a section headed Lyrics and Reveries. Its first titles include In Front of the Landscape, Channel Firing, The Convergence of the Twain, and The Ghost of the Past.
un-un-res-eighth-progress-report-of-the-:
Sierra Leone's fragile peace is tracked in the eighth progress report of the Secretary-General on the United Nations Observer Mission there, filed in 1999 as document S/1999/1003. The small observer mission, called UNOMSIL, watched a country emerging from civil war. A peace deal signed at Lomé that year gave the mission fresh duties.

The report covers security, the return of refugees, and plans to disarm fighters. It notes where the peace held and where armed groups still posed a threat. Such reports gave the Security Council the facts it used to extend or reshape the mission.

Late 1998 in Sierra Leone is covered by the second progress report of the Secretary-General on the United Nations Observer Mission there, document S/1998/960. The mission, UNOMSIL, was watching a state restored to elected rule but still hunted by rebel groups. Fighting in the provinces was growing worse as the year closed.

The report tracks security incidents, the work of West African troops backing the government, and the state of aid for civilians. It warns that rebel strength was rising fast. Within weeks, rebels would attack the capital itself, a turn this report helps readers foresee.
